name: Habakkuk

overview.author: Habakkuk the prophet (1:1).
overview.date: Probably about 609–605 BC, shortly before the Babylonians (Chaldeans) invaded Judah.
overview.audience: Judah, though the book is mostly a dialogue between the prophet and God.
overview.setting: Judah under Jehoiakim was full of violence and injustice, and Babylon was rising as a world power.
overview.purpose: To wrestle honestly with God’s ways in judgment, and to show that the righteous live by faith, trusting and rejoicing in God even when circumstances collapse.
overview.structure: Habakkuk’s first complaint and God’s answer (1:1–11), the second complaint (1:12–2:1), God’s answer with five woes (2:2–20), and Habakkuk’s prayer of faith (3).

items.title: The righteous shall live by faith

themes.title: Honest Questions
themes.text: Habakkuk brings his confusion directly to God.

themes.title: God’s Sovereignty
themes.text: God raises up Babylon for His purposes and will also judge it.

themes.title: Faith
themes.text: “The righteous shall live by his faith” (2:4).

themes.title: Patience
themes.text: “If it seems slow, wait for it; it will surely come” (2:3).

themes.title: Judgment on Pride
themes.text: Five woes condemn greed, violence, exploitation, and idolatry.

themes.title: God’s Glory
themes.text: “The earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD” (2:14).

themes.title: Joy in Hardship
themes.text: Habakkuk rejoices in God even with no figs, fruit, or flocks (3:17–18).

keyVerses.quote: O LORD, how long shall I cry for help, and you will not hear?
But the righteous shall live by his faith.
For the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD as the waters cover the sea.
The LORD is in his holy temple; let all the earth keep silence before him.
Yet I will rejoice in the LORD; I will take joy in the God of my salvation.

christInBook.text: Paul builds the gospel of justification by faith on this verse (Romans 1:17; Galatians 3:11; Hebrews 10:38).
God going out “for the salvation of your anointed” points to Christ’s victory.
The knowledge of God’s glory fills the earth through the gospel of Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6).

crossReferences.note: No one is justified by the law.
Wrestling with the prosperity of the wicked.

reflection: What “How long?” questions are you bringing to God right now?
How does Habakkuk model honest prayer that still trusts God?
What does it mean in daily life to “live by faith” (2:4)?
What vision or promise of God are you waiting for (2:3)?
Write your own version of 3:17–18, naming what you lack yet choosing to rejoice.

chapterList.title: How Long, O LORD?
chapterList.summary: Habakkuk complains: “How long shall I cry for help, and you will not hear?” Violence and injustice fill Judah. God answers that He is raising up the Chaldeans, a fierce nation, to judge Judah. Habakkuk is shocked: how can a holy God use people more wicked than Judah?
questions: Why was God’s answer so surprising (1:5–6)?
How does Habakkuk hold onto God’s character while questioning (1:12–13)?

chapterList.title: The Righteous Shall Live by Faith
chapterList.summary: Habakkuk stations himself to watch. God says, “Write the vision; make it plain.” It will surely come. The proud soul is not upright, “but the righteous shall live by his faith.” Five woes condemn Babylon’s greed, unjust gain, violence, degradation of others, and idolatry. “The LORD is in his holy temple; let all the earth keep silence before him.”
questions: Why does God tell Habakkuk to write the vision (2:2–3)?
What contrast does 2:18–20 draw between idols and God?

chapterList.title: Yet I Will Rejoice
chapterList.summary: Habakkuk prays, “In wrath remember mercy.” He recounts God’s mighty acts, like the Exodus, in which God marched out to save His people. He trembles, but resolves: “Though the fig tree should not blossom... yet I will rejoice in the LORD... God, the Lord, is my strength; he makes my feet like the deer’s.”
questions: Why does remembering God’s past acts help Habakkuk?
What does it mean to “remember mercy” in wrath (3:2)?
How is joy in 3:17–19 possible when everything fails?

tagline: From “How long?” to “Yet I will rejoice”: living by faith
readingPlan: 3 chapters: one chapter a day takes 3 days; two a day takes about 2 days. For each chapter, read it on ESV.org, then come back here for the summary, questions, and your notes.
